identity.name: CAMPUS ACTIVEWEAR LIMITED
identity.industry: Footwear / Premium Activewear & Distribution-Led Consumer Brands

summary.oneLiner: One of India's largest and fastest-growing Sports Athleisure (S&A) footwear and apparel companies by both value and volume, built on a design-led, vertically integrated manufacturing and omnichannel distribution platform.
summary.business: Campus Activewear designs, manufactures, markets, sells and distributes sports and athleisure footwear, apparel and accessories (socks, backpacks, caps, belts) for men, women and children, sold under the Campus brand and its new sub-brand ELAN by Campus. It serves a broad Indian consumer base across Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities through e-commerce platforms, authorised distributors, exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) and multi-brand outlets (MBOs), with a small export presence.

currentContext.strengths: Design innovation: in-house design team of 30+ professionals with 1,600+ active styles in circulation and 240+ new designs introduced in FY26|Vertically integrated supply chain spanning in-house sole and upper manufacturing, enabling a demand-input-to-warehouse lead time of 60-90 days versus an industry average of 90-120 days|Scaled omnichannel distribution network of 29,000+ retail touchpoints across 800 districts in 28 states, supported by 260+ distributors, 300 EBOs and 2,300+ large-format-store counters|Culture-led brand building with celebrity-fronted campaigns (Vicky Kaushal, Kriti Sanon) driving rising brand-health metrics (top-of-mind awareness, spontaneous awareness, consideration)|Approximately 90% domestic raw-material sourcing and 100% in-house final assembly, supporting cost control and supply resilience
currentContext.strategies: In FY27, scale the new apparel category thoughtfully, deepen the sneaker and women's franchises, extend presence in Western and Southern India, and continue investing in technology, design and talent.|Deliberate choice of profitability before proliferation in offline retail: held EBO count near 300, corrected store-level unit economics and strengthened franchise partner returns before resuming EBO expansion.|Completed pivot of the online business from an outright to a marketplace-led model, giving stronger control and better realisations, while remaining the leading footwear brand on major e-commerce and quick-commerce platforms.|Extension into sports athleisure apparel (launched January 2026 across 60+ EBOs, the brand website, Amazon and Myntra) as a natural extension of design capability, brand equity and distribution network, being scaled with a disciplined, measured approach.|Continued investment in digital and operational agility (SAP backbone, DMS-led replenishment, field-force applications, daily online replenishment) to move from a made-to-stock toward a made-to-order model.|The Company has not issued any debt instruments or non-convertible securities; Crisil Ratings revised its outlook on the Company's long-term bank facilities to 'Positive' from 'Stable' during the year, reaffirming 'Crisil A+' (long-term) and 'Crisil A1' (short-term). Employee ownership is maintained through two Employee Stock Option Plans (ESOP 2021 and ESOP 2021 - Vision Pool). BRSR reporting confirms the Company has no subsidiaries or associates.
currentContext.expansion: Commercial production of premium uppers commenced at the Pantnagar facility in January 2026, adding to the Company's integrated premium capacity, while the Paonta Sahib upper facility stabilised fully during FY26. In January 2026 the Company also launched a new athleisure apparel range, initially across 60+ Exclusive Brand Outlets, the brand website and on Amazon/Myntra, as a natural extension of its design capability, brand equity and distribution network. Management states that land and infrastructure are already in place to add manufacturing capacity quickly as demand grows.
currentContext.mdna: India's per capita footwear consumption remains well below global averages, with a young, increasingly fitness-conscious consumer base steadily trading up to branded products.|GST rationalisation during the year was a structural reform for the footwear category; the industry has yet to feel its full demand impact, and management expects it to act as a tailwind as the benefit flows through.|Sports and Athleisure (S&A) has emerged as the fastest-growing footwear segment in India, now accounting for more than two-thirds of the overall market.|Branded footwear is expected to achieve parity with the traditionally dominant unbranded segment as organised retail (EBOs, large-format stores, e-commerce) gains traction, supported by 100% FDI and Footwear Park development.|Premiumisation and a richer product mix (led by the sneaker portfolio) are lifting average selling price and margin, aided by operating leverage and a higher share of premium SKUs.|Demand across the footwear industry remained softer than anticipated during the year, with discretionary spending yet to recover fully.

risks.note: Stiff competition from well-resourced global athletic footwear brands operating in India and emerging domestic D2C players; aggressive pricing, promotional intensity and rapid product iteration by competitors can compress margins and raise customer acquisition costs.

Operational efficiency depends on consistent availability of high-quality inputs (EVA, PU, synthetic uppers, adhesives); disruption or quality deterioration in the supply chain could cause production delays, higher costs and lower consumer satisfaction.

Input costs are sensitive to global commodity movements, particularly petrochemical derivatives underpinning synthetic materials; sharp cost increases may compress margins if not passed through to consumers in a timely manner.

Maintaining product relevance in a market shaped by rapidly shifting consumer style preferences requires sustained design innovation and responsive supply chain execution; misreading trend direction could hurt sales velocity and inventory utilisation.

Changes in import duties, BIS compliance standards, GST structures and other regulatory frameworks can alter the Company's cost base and necessitate pricing adjustments; the unresolved inverted-duty structure on certain raw materials remains a cost overhang, against which refund claims have begun to be filed.

Inflation spikes, interest rate increases, currency depreciation or geopolitical disruptions can weaken consumer sentiment and reduce discretionary spending, directly impacting demand for branded and aspirational products.
Proliferation of counterfeit and imitation products, particularly in mass-market and online channels, poses a risk to brand integrity, consumer trust and revenue.
As the Company expands its digital and D2C operations, managing cybersecurity risk and consumer data privacy remains a critical area requiring sustained investment and vigilance.

one-line thesis: Campus delivered 16% revenue growth and 40% PAT growth in Q2FY26 driven by premium segment expansion (ASP up 8%) and distribution channel strength, with normalized EBITDA margin at 16% despite phasing in marketing spend; the key inflection is in-house upper capacity expansion enabling IP control and premium pricing, positioning the company to capture share from unorganized players post-GST rationalization.
financial scorecard: Revenue: +16% YoY to INR 387cr; EBITDA: +140bps to 14% (normalized: 16% after stripping 200bps phasing in A&P); PAT: +40% YoY to INR 20cr (rptd); Order book: Not disclosed; Net debt: Increased due to working capital build for seasonality and Pant Nagar lease, but expected to normalize by FY26 end
guidance: Revenue growth: Double-digit for FY26; Margin: Targeting 16-17% EBITDA margin long-term; Order inflow: Not disclosed; Capex/commissioning: INR 110-115cr in FY26 for Pant Nagar upper plant (3L pairs/month capacity), commissioning by Q4FY26
segment / subsidiary detail: Premium segment (INR 1,500+): 57.2% of mix (+12pp YoY); Women's: 16.2% of revenue (+2pp YoY); Kids: 4-5%; Accessories: 2-3%; Online: 5.7% growth (impacted by BBD timing shift); Distribution: 20% growth; Export: Nascent, under own brand, pilot in Sri Lanka/Morocco
growth verticals / optionality: Apparel launch (pilot in 60 EBOs in Q3FY26); Export scaling (targeting 5-10% revenue in 2-3 years); Premium sneaker volume growth (100%+ YoY); LFS and defense channel expansion
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin improved to 53.9% (up 110bps) due to premium mix and ASP increase; EBITDA margin 14% (rptd), 16% normalized after removing 200bps A&P phasing; Cost of outsourced uppers higher than in-house; Labor cost spike in Haridwar 2 plant (0.4% margin drag) to be neutralized by FY26 end
capex / expansion: FY26 capex: INR 110-115cr for Pant Nagar upper plant (land + building); Total 3-year capex plan: INR 230cr (incl. 2 more upper lines + assembly); Maintenance capex: INR 40-50cr (stores, IT, molds); Total FY26 capex: ~INR 150-165cr
capital allocation: Prioritizing capex for in-house upper/sole capacity to enable premiumization and IP protection; Maintaining strong ROCE (16.6%) and ROE (18%); Net debt expected to normalize by FY26 end; No dividend guidance disclosed
risks & watch-items: Execution risk in Pant Nagar ramp-up; Delay in export market adoption; Oversupply in unorganized segment post-GST; High working capital intensity during peak season; Apparel pilot failure
management quality / tone: Confident and strategic; focused on premiumization, capacity control, and long-term brand building; optimistic on GST tailwind and export potential; transparent on phasing and one-offs; no overpromising on margins or export targets
non-obvious takeaways: The 8% ASP growth was achieved despite a 12-15% revenue reduction from Flipkart/Myntra business model shift (freight now charged to consumer), indicating true underlying pricing power; Inventory build is seasonal and structural (MSME payment terms tightened to 45 days), not channel stuffing
challenges → beneficiaries & losers:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unorganized players losing price advantage post-GST | Campus Activewear Limited | beneficiary | High | Structured premiumization and in-house capacity create sustainable moat against informal sector |
| Bata and other organized players with legacy cost structures | Campus Activewear Limited | beneficiary | Medium | Campus' China/Vietnam-grade tech and lower labor cost enable faster premiumization |

themes.title: Consumption revival & FMCG premiumization
themes.need: Rural recovery, GST 2.0 and premiumization still frame the theme, but Q1FY27 rewarded portfolio SHAPE over volume. TATACONSUM's growth businesses hit INR 1,300cr (+47%) and are now 36% of India - larger than either salt (>INR 1,000cr) or tea & coffee (INR 1,200cr), with Sampann +58%, RTD +41% and Capital Foods INR 232cr (+40%) - while India tea revenue fell 4% on +2% volume as lower tea costs were deliberately passed back (tea inflation is now running 7-10% with most buying still ahead, so that inverts next year). PGHH shows the margin route: FY26 sales roughly flat at ~INR 4,300cr but PAT +19% to ~INR 850cr and ~100bps of structural margin from INR 86cr of productivity savings, absorbing crude and resin each up 30-50% with no stock-outs. The cautionary tale is licensed brands - JYOTHYLAB lost the Pril and Fa licences when Henkel did not renew (all manufacturing and selling stopped 1-June; Pril was ~7-8% of revenue, ~INR 225-240cr) and has filed SIAC arbitration. MARICO/DABUR/GODREJCP/COLPAL/EMAMILTD ride distribution + premium mix; VBL on beverage route-to-market; BIKAJI/GOPAL/BECTORFOOD on branded snacks; ORKLAINDIA took a 4% blended price increase in Q4 plus premium mix to a 16.9% EBITDA margin.
themes.driver: GST 2.0 demand pull-through; rural volume recovery; festive/wedding restocking; commodity pass-back timing; JYOTHYLAB's ~7-8% revenue hole and the SIAC arbitration.
